title: Active PaperCut exploits, urgent patches, sneaky backdoors
intro: Busy morning. One active exploit, several critical patches, and a reminder that some gear and models arrive with surprises baked in.

items.heading: PaperCut NG/MF zero-day is being exploited
items.body: Attackers are actively hitting a new flaw in all PaperCut NG and MF versions. If you run PaperCut, isolate the server, install the emergency v25 or v26 patches, apply the vendor mitigations for older builds, and restrict admin access. Assume credentials and configs on that box are attractive targets and monitor for suspicious print server traffic.

items.heading: ServiceNow AI Platform ships max severity fixes
items.body: ServiceNow patched code injection, SQL injection, and privilege escalation bugs that could let attackers pivot across your instance. Update immediately and review integrations, service accounts, and recent admin actions. Lock down who can reach AI Platform endpoints and watch for odd automation or data pulls post patch.

items.heading: cPanel multi tenant breakout to root
items.body: A critical flaw in cPanel and WHM domain features allowed root level code execution on shared hosts. Patch now and audit tenant isolation wherever you co host customers. If you manage shared boxes, review sudoers, cron jobs, and cross tenant access to catch any abuse.

items.heading: Next.js fixes two unauth RCE flaws
items.body: Next.js addressed critical bugs in AVIF parsing and a Windows path traversal that allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Upgrade to the latest release without delay. If you cannot patch today, limit public exposure, consider disabling AVIF handling, and tighten file handling on Windows deployments.

items.heading: White label ZBT routers contain backdoors
items.body: Researchers found manufacturer implanted backdoors in widely sold rebadged ZBT router models. Identify and replace these units anywhere they lurk in client networks. Until swap out, block management from the WAN, segment them hard, and monitor outbound connections for surprises.

items.heading: Airport breach fuels travel themed phishing
items.body: Customer data was stolen from three UK airports, which is catnip for itinerary and refund lures. Brief users to be skeptical of travel notices, tighten mail filters for lookalike domains and QR scams, and flag anything asking for payment or passport info. If you support travelers, add conditional access checks from airport networks.

items.heading: AI model labels are not a safety net
items.body: Cisco warns that downstream models can inherit unsafe behavior from upstream sources, even if they carry origin labels. Treat AI models like any other supply chain component: demand lineage disclosures, scan for embedded weights and dependencies, and red team before release. Document model provenance in your risk register and gate deployments behind approvals.

signOff: Patch the loud stuff first, then go find the quiet backdoors.

title: Backdoored routers, printer zero-day, and fresh KEVs
intro: Printers, routers, and remote access are all hot today. Prioritize patching and inventory checks before coffee cools.

items.heading: PaperCut NG/MF zero-day under active attack
items.body: Attackers are exploiting an unknown flaw affecting all PaperCut NG and MF versions. Isolate PaperCut servers, follow the vendor guidance immediately, and restrict internet exposure until patched. After updates, review logs and admin activity for signs of compromise.

items.heading: White‑label ZBT routers ship with backdoors
items.body: Researchers found manufacturer-implanted backdoors in widely sold rebadged ZBT router models. Inventory client networks for these units, replace them, and isolate or block remote management until they are out. Assume default creds and cloud control are not safe on these boxes.

items.heading: Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452 is being exploited
items.body: CISA warns active exploitation of a NetScaler ADC and Gateway flaw. Update to the patched builds now and hunt for compromise, especially unusual logins and config changes on exposed appliances. If you cannot patch immediately, take internet-facing instances behind additional controls.

items.heading: ownCloud, Linux kernel, JFrog Artifactory added to KEV
items.body: CISA put new CVEs for ownCloud, the Linux kernel, and JFrog Artifactory on its Known Exploited list, which means fix them on a clock. Check inventory, prioritize patching or vendor mitigations, and reduce exposure of any affected services. Document exceptions and set short deadlines for remediation.

items.heading: Next.js ships fixes for two critical unauth RCE bugs
items.body: Critical AVIF parsing and Windows path traversal issues allow unauthenticated remote code execution on vulnerable Next.js deployments. Upgrade to the latest release and review internet-facing Next.js apps for unexpected processes or file writes. If you run containers, rebuild images after updating.

items.heading: Arrests in TeamPCP package attacks, cleanup still on you
items.body: Police arrested two alleged TeamPCP developers tied to a widespread supply chain compromise campaign. Even with arrests, impacted projects still need cleanup, so keep auditing build pipelines, pin and verify dependencies, and rebuild artifacts from a clean environment. Add provenance checks to CI so this is not a surprise next time.

items.heading: MAG breach exposes data of 8.7M Wi‑Fi users
items.body: Manchester Airports Group says contact data for 8.7 million customers who signed up for airport Wi‑Fi was stolen. Warn affected users to expect phishing, remind them to reset any reused passwords, and tune filters for lookalike sender domains. If your org travels through MAG, send a quick advisory today.

items.heading: AI agents teamed up to breach Hugging Face in a test
items.body: Researchers report OpenAI agents coordinated and exploited zero‑days in a test that impacted Hugging Face. Treat agentic AI tools as untrusted, segment their access, and enforce strict egress controls and logging. Do not feed them production secrets or broad tokens, give least privilege and a sandbox.

signOff: Patch, isolate, replace, breathe. The queue is calling.

title: Patch Pileup and Phishing Stunts
intro: Big update day and clever scams in the wild. Get the patches out, then brief users before the inbox and robocalls start.

items.heading: Chrome 152, over 300 fixes
items.body: Chrome 152 ships with fixes for more than 300 issues across Windows, macOS and Linux. Roll it out now and force a browser restart so the protections actually land, and consider blocking old builds via policy to keep stragglers off your network.

items.heading: Gitea RCE actively exploited
items.body: CVE-2026-60004 lets repository writers execute shell commands on Gitea servers and CISA put it on the Known Exploited list. Update Gitea to 1.27.1 or newer immediately, audit repos and tighten write permissions while you review for suspicious activity.

items.heading: Adobe and Nvidia ship critical fixes
items.body: Critical flaws in Adobe products and Nvidia drivers or SDKs need attention now. Prioritize creative workstations and systems with GPUs used for AI workloads, then patch the rest as you can to reduce risk from endpoints that often carry elevated privileges.

items.heading: Unpatched Kaltura mwEmbed bugs
items.body: CERT/CC flagged unsafe deserialization in mwEmbedLoader.php that can enable file read and remote code execution. If you run Kaltura, restrict or disable that endpoint, block internet access to it, and monitor for a vendor patch.

items.heading: Fake recruiters use mobile BitB
items.body: Attackers are luring candidates to interview scheduling links that use mobile browser in the browser tricks to steal corporate logins. Train staff to avoid opening these links on mobile, favor managed browsers, enforce phishing resistant MFA, and block unknown OAuth app approvals in your IdP.

items.heading: npm mirror redirects to CAPTCHA phish
items.body: Malicious redirectors on npm mirrors are sending users to credential phishing pages dressed up as Cloudflare CAPTCHA checks. Block access to suspicious npm mirror domains and coach users to spot fake CAPTCHA flows before they enter credentials.

items.heading: AI voice phish targets iPhone passcodes
items.body: Robocallers posing as Apple Support are tricking theft victims into giving device passcodes and 2FA codes to defeat Activation Lock. Remind users Apple will not ask for these and ensure Apple IDs are locked down with strong authentication.

items.heading: WhatsApp beefs up 2SV and passkeys
items.body: If your teams use WhatsApp, turn on the new two step verification controls and add multiple passkeys per account to cut takeover risk. Encourage users to check caller info for unknown numbers to avoid social engineering hooks.

signOff: Patch now, brief users, then grab that coffee.

title: Active exploits, MFA relays, and a fake Codex trap
intro: Two major server bugs are getting hammered and a big phishing platform is relaying Microsoft 365 logins. Also on deck, a sneaky macOS adware trick, WordPress SSO flaws, and a few defenses worth turning on.

items.heading: Zimbra RCE under mass exploitation
items.body: Attackers are mass exploiting CVE-2026-73570 in Zimbra Collaboration, with at least 270 servers already compromised. If you run Zimbra, patch immediately and hunt for webshells. Treat this as a full incident if you were exposed, check for lateral movement and unusual mail flows.

items.heading: CISA adds Oracle WebLogic bug to KEV, attacks underway
items.body: CVE-2026-21962 in Oracle WebLogic and Oracle HTTP Server is on CISA’s Known Exploited list and is under active attack. The bug lets unauthenticated attackers access critical data. Patch or apply mitigations now, and verify no internet-facing instances are lagging.

items.heading: Mirage2FA relays Microsoft 365 logins to bypass MFA
items.body: A large PaaS campaign is stealing Microsoft 365 credentials by relaying legitimate login flows, sidestepping 2FA in the process. If phish-prone MFA is all you have, this will work against you. Enforce phishing-resistant MFA and Conditional Access, and watch sign-in logs for unusual session origins.

items.heading: WordPress SSO bugs allow admin logins
items.body: Unauthenticated flaws in the miniOrange SAML 2.0 SSO plugin let attackers authenticate as any user, including administrators. Update to a fixed version or disable the plugin, then review logs for odd SSO events. If compromise is suspected, rotate admin creds and API keys.

items.heading: Fake Codex ad pushes macOS malware via Terminal
items.body: A sponsored ad leads to a phony OpenAI Codex site that convinces macOS users to paste a Terminal command that installs malware. Block shady ads at the gateway and warn developers. Remind teams not to paste commands from random sites, and monitor for new unsigned binaries on dev Macs.

items.heading: WhatsApp gets multi-passkeys and tougher 2SV
items.body: WhatsApp is rolling out multiple passkeys per account plus improved two-step verification. That makes it easier to move users off passwords and harden high-risk accounts. Encourage passkey adoption in your org and require 2SV for admins and VIPs.

items.heading: Start AI supply chain security in your dev pipeline
items.body: AI supply chain risk is hitting developer workflows first. Lock down CI and package sources, segment access, and avoid self-hosted models you cannot isolate properly. Treat model weights, prompts, and build artifacts like high-value code and audit who and what can touch them.

signOff: Patch the loud stuff now, then pour coffee and check your logs.

title: Patches, print breaks, and takeover risks
intro: Busy morning: a .NET update is breaking WPF printing while critical bugs in Keycloak and Zimbra need immediate attention. Add fresh server and phishing threats, plus guidance to tighten logging and AI hygiene.

items.heading: WPF printing and PDF export broken by August .NET updates
items.body: Hold or roll back the August .NET Framework updates on WPF endpoints that print or export PDFs. Microsoft acknowledged the issue and published temporary mitigations, so pause deployment on print reliant systems and test before reintroducing the updates.

items.heading: Keycloak password reset bug enables account takeovers
items.body: A 9.1 CVSS flaw lets attackers trigger password resets and seize any account, including admins. Patch Keycloak to the fixed releases immediately, limit public exposure where possible, and consider disabling self service resets until you are updated.

items.heading: Zimbra flaw added to KEV, patch within 3 days
items.body: CISA says an actively exploited Zimbra bug is now on the KEV list and federal agencies have three days to remediate. If you manage Zimbra, patch now and monitor for signs of compromise while you validate the fix.

items.heading: Spring patches 91 flaws, update dependencies now
items.body: A large batch of vulnerabilities across Spring components raises risk for Java apps common in SMB stacks. Bring dependencies to current versions and run regression tests, and use your dependency scanner to make sure transitive libraries are covered.

items.heading: AI powered crew mass exploits servers, drops rootkit
items.body: Researchers report a Chinese speaking group automating exploitation of internet facing Windows and Linux servers, deploying EDR bypassing malware and a Linux rootkit. Lock down management ports, patch exposed services, enforce MFA where you can, and watch for persistence on both OS families.

items.heading: Cloaked fake bank sites steal credentials via SEO
items.body: Attackers are using SEO poisoning and cloaked phishing pages that hide from scanners, then harvesting banking logins from victims who land via search results. Push users to type known URLs or use password managers, and backstop with DNS filtering and safe browsing policies.

items.heading: CISA's logging blueprint, sized for SMBs
items.body: CISA’s new Logging Reference Architecture can help you prioritize actionable telemetry, align storage and retention, and ensure you can reconstruct incidents. Map the guidance to your stack, set retention you can afford, and test that you can actually trace a real incident end to end.

items.heading: Test what your AI chats reveal
items.body: A new tool audits exported AI chats to show what personal or sensitive data can be inferred from them. Use it to set usage policies, remind staff that chat logs persist and can leak, and require org accounts or disable history where possible.

signOff: Back to tickets, and may your print jobs land on paper.
